items.title: $ONDS We see your tired agenda, but just for funsies, I’ll retort. The key word, my dear bear, is ACCRETIVE! The uneducated and lazy like to
items.content_excerpt: $ONDS We see your tired agenda, but just for funsies, I’ll retort. The key word, my dear bear, is ACCRETIVE! The uneducated and lazy like to focus on near-term costs and ownership percentages without understanding the bigger picture of what a company is building for the future. The thesis is accretive growth: using equity strategically to expand capabilities, acquire businesses, and build long-term value that can outpace the growth in shares outstanding. Tesla, Amazon, and other successful growth companies demonstrate why investors shouldn’t automatically equate a growing share count with a failed strategy. What matters is what the company builds, how well management executes, and whether the resulting business becomes more valuable on a per-share basis. I’m focused on what Ondas is building, the markets it’s positioned to capture, and the potential for its growth strategy to prove accretive over time. You can count shares all day. I’m watching the bigger picture.

items.title: $NVDA at $229.28 sits inside our range ($106.05 to $265.75, from 2 models), but only because the next two years are so strong. Guidance carr
items.content_excerpt: $NVDA at $229.28 sits inside our range ($106.05 to $265.75, from 2 models), but only because the next two years are so strong. Guidance carries most of it: FY27 roughly +86%, FY28 ~+70%. Our model then lets growth fall to 10%, 5%, 3% with margins easing into the low 50s, and averages 30.4% a year over five years. Hold margins where they are and price alone asks for more than 25% a year. So the bear case isn't the next two years. It's whether the capex cycle has a down leg after FY28. Things that would show it: hyperscaler capex guides flattening, more chips bought with debt, and the memory-cost margin reset (gross margin guided to 71-72% in Q4). Not investment advice.

items.content_excerpt: $TSLA Valuation Baseline: Trades at a persistent valuation premium relative to legacy automotive OEMs and general mega-cap industrials. ​The Drivers: High market expectations tied to non-automotive drivers—specifically Full Self-Driving (FSD), robotaxis, energy storage growth, and humanoid robotics. ​CAPE Dynamics: Tesla's 10-year earnings record spans early production struggles, low-margin scale phases, and volatile gross margins. While core EV sales face cyclical auto pressures, the stock price reflects tech-like option value, driving a multi-year CAPE divergence. ​Downturn Sensitivity: High beta stock with pronounced implied volatility swings. Margin pressure or delays in autonomous commercialization leave the equity vulnerable during broader risk-off pullbacks.

items.content_excerpt: Flagship neoclouds If the hyperscalers were adequate, neoclouds wouldn’t be proliferating. Modal, a startup operating virtual sandboxes where AI agents work independent of main IT environments, went from running on the hyperscalers to signing up with the major neoclouds, and now it uses 25 of them, said CEO Erik Bernhardsson. “You can get a few hundred GPUs or maybe a thousand, but at our scale, we needed way more GPUs,” he said. The hyperscalers themselves are also chasing the neoclouds. Google and Microsoft have started tapping CoreWeave, even as they all compete with one another. $CRWV $MSFT $NVDA

items.content_excerpt: Silicon Valley’s AI boom is reshaping the tech industry as companies intensify their desperate hunt for computing power, specialized chips, infrastructure and top talent. Fierce competitors are increasingly forming unexpected alliances, while senior executives are personally stepping in to secure the resources needed to develop and deploy increasingly powerful AI models. The shortage of computing capacity has become a strategic bottleneck, forcing companies to rethink traditional partnerships and compete aggressively for the technology and expertise required to stay ahead. The battle for talent is equally intense. Google, eager to bring pioneering AI researcher Noam Shazeer back into its organization, paid $2.7 billion in 2024 to bring him back after he left to launch his own company. Shazeer returned to work on cutting-edge projects, including Gemini, Google's most advanced AI technology. $GOOGL

items.content_excerpt: $BTC.X $MSTR $ETH.X $COIN $BMNR 💡 "Most watched level Globally". "Self-fulfilling". Just saying... 😏 61.8% Level (The Golden Ratio): This is considered the ultimate "make or break" line for a trend. It is the most watched Fibonacci level globally. If the price pulls back here and bounces, the original trend is still considered very healthy and strong. In trading terminology, "recovery" here means the market is trying to find a floor or ceiling to stage a comeback. This zone represents a crucial psychological and technical battlefield for traders. 61% to 78% recovery (more precisely, the 61.8% to 78.6% zone) refers to a deep price pullback (retracement) where an asset gives back a significant portion of its previous structural move before attempting to resume its original trend. "It might make sense just to get some in case it catches on. If enough people think the same way, that becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy" -Satoshi Nakamoto 01.03.2009

items.content_excerpt: GlobalFoundries announced a five-year, $2 billion manufacturing agreement with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., under which it will produce silicon interposers at its Malta, New York facility to support TSMC’s advanced CoWoS packaging ecosystem. Silicon interposers are critical components in high-performance AI chip packages, enabling high-speed communication between processors and memory. The agreement also establishes a framework to expand production capacity as demand grows, with GlobalFoundries incorporating embedded deep-trench capacitor technology into the manufacturing process. The deal provides the company with a direct, revenue-generating opportunity tied to the expanding AI infrastructure supply chain. BNP Paribas also upgraded GlobalFoundries to Hold, reversing a previous downgrade, while a recent Form 4 filing reflected routine RSU vesting and tax withholding rather than discretionary insider buying. $GFS $TSM

items.content_excerpt: $COHR Coherent was among the worst performers in the S&P 500 on Thursday: down 9.63% to 302.35, off a 334.56 prior close. Barron's named it with Bloom Energy, Vistra, Lumentum, Super Micro and Intel among the index's worst names on the day. The trigger was not Coherent-specific. The FT reported OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue run-rate was approaching 50 billion at end-September, about 20 billion below what it had previously signaled. The PHLX Semiconductor index fell 4.2% and the S&P tech sector dropped 2%. One level down: this is the optics leverage at work. Data center and communications is about 79% of revenue, 1.6 billion last quarter, up 58.6% YoY. It is a pure-play read on hyperscaler AI capex. Nothing in the FT report touches actual capex budgets. OpenAI has not confirmed the figure, and no hyperscaler has cut spending. Coherent's own demand visibility is order-book driven. A demand-scare de-rating on the most exposed name, not a data point.

It is the most watched Fibonacci level globally. If the price pulls back here and bounces, the original trend is still considered very healthy and strong. In trading terminology, "recovery" here means the market is trying to find a floor or ceiling to stage a comeback. This zone represents a crucial psychological and technical battlefield for traders. 61% to 78% recovery (more precisely, the 61.8% to 78.6% zone) refers to a deep price pullback (retracement) where an asset gives back a significant portion of its previous structural move before attempting to resume its original trend. The deal provides the company with a direct, revenue-generating opportunity tied to the expanding AI infrastructure supply chain.
